documents.title: AI 101 - Campus Edition
documents.stance_why: The page says "neither UCSB nor the UC system has a formal policy" and tells each instructor to decide ("What is the AI policy in your course?"), so it sets no stance itself and hands the decision to instructors.
documents.summary: Teaching-center explainer on generative AI. It gives scenarios and sample policies for instructors, notes Student Conduct treats unapproved AI as plagiarism, and offers study prompts and privacy tips.

units.why: The page defines Gen AI as a "Subset of AI that focuses on creating new data or content", setting what it discusses. P61.
units.anchor: Subset of AI that focuses on creating new data or content

units.why: The page says Gen AI "provides innovative and effective ways to approach the learning process", naming a benefit with no rule. P87.
units.anchor: Gen AI provides innovative and effective ways to approach the learning process
units.fit_note: Also says it requires thoughtful and responsible engagement.
units.resolution_why: Only coder A found this. The page says Gen AI 'provides innovative and effective ways to approach the learning process' but 'requires thoughtful and responsible engagement'. That is a stated benefit and caution about AI in learning, a real rationale statement, so kept as P87 informs.

units.why: Symposium recordings are noted to highlight "issues of academic integrity, bias, and inequities". That names harms, P53.
units.anchor: these presentations also highlight issues of academic integrity, bias, and inequities
units.resolution_why: Only coder A found this. The page says the symposium presentations 'highlight issues of academic integrity, bias, and inequities'. It explains concerns about AI use and is kept as a rationale statement (P53).

units.why: The page reports UCUES survey results on student AI use ("38% used Gen AI at least several times per month"), which is evidence on use, P55.
units.anchor: 38% used Gen AI at least several times per month.
units.frag_end: at least several times per month.
units.fit_note: Evidence concerns how often students use AI and how they view policies, not learning outcomes. / Cites survey data on usage and perception, not learning outcomes.
units.resolution_why: Same passage (UCUES survey figures). Actor differed: A said all, B said admin. The data are given to all readers of the page, not addressed to an office, so actor is all. Phase over-time and P55 agreed.

units.why: "creating policies around AI use are complicated because it is rapidly evolving" says the policy area keeps changing, P54.
units.anchor: creating policies around AI use are complicated because it is rapidly evolving
units.fit_note: Notes change; does not commit to revising a UCSB policy. / Notes evolution as difficulty; no commitment to revisit.
units.resolution_why: Same sentence ('creating policies around AI use are complicated because it is rapidly evolving'). Actor differed: A all, B instructor. It is a general observation, not an instruction to instructors, so actor is all. Phase over-time and P54 agreed; it does not commit UCSB to revise a policy (see fit_note).

units.why: The page states "neither UCSB nor the UC system has a formal policy on generative AI in teaching and learning contexts". This leaves the decision to instructors, P04.
units.anchor: neither UCSB nor the UC system has a formal policy on generative AI
units.fit_note: Says no formal institutional policy exists; the delegation to instructors is implied by the surrounding advice.
units.resolution_why: Same sentence ('neither UCSB nor the UC system has a formal policy'). Phase differed: A general, B before-course. The sentence states a fact about the institution's policy status, not a step in designing a course, so phase is general. Actor instructor and P04 agreed: the sentence sits under 'Instructors: Policies and Guidance' and leaves the rule to each instructor.

units.why: Instructors who are unsure how to begin are told to consider "what you would do if the following scenarios occurred" (translation, summarizing, quiz practice, a student-built tutor bot, coding and debugging, unequal paid access). This prompts each instructor to decide per scenario, P04.
units.anchor: consider what you would do if the following scenarios occurred in your course

units.why: OTL says it "compiled sample Generative AI policies that you can adapt for your course and assignments", a support for instructors writing statements. P63.
units.anchor: sample Generative AI policies that you can adapt for your course and assignments
units.fit_note: Sample policy language rather than workshops.
units.resolution_why: Same sentence ('OTL has compiled sample Generative AI policies that you can adapt'). A: instructor, may. B: admin, informs. The sentence is addressed to instructors ('you can adapt') and offers a permission, so instructor and may. P63 agreed.

units.why: Instructors are invited to "meet with an Instructional Consultant at OTL for feedback on your policy". P63.
units.anchor: meet with an Instructional Consultant at OTL for feedback on your policy
units.resolution_why: Same sentence ('Please meet with an Instructional Consultant at OTL for feedback on your policy'). A: may. B: should, actor admin. The invitation is addressed to instructors ('your policy') and is offered 'if you'd like to think through' further scenarios, so it is a permission: instructor, may. P63 agreed.

units.why: Quotes Student Conduct standards that academic dishonesty includes 'utilizing artificial intelligence programs without prior approval from the instructor' and 'Unauthorized use of artificial intelligence programs'. Misconduct classification: P36.
units.anchor: utilizing artificial intelligence programs without prior approval from the instructor
units.resolution_why: Coder A coded the second quotation of the Student Conduct rule ('Unauthorized use of artificial intelligence programs to complete coursework', all, when-misuse, informs, prohibit); coder B coded the first quotation ('utilizing artificial intelligence programs without prior approval from the instructor', student, when-misuse, must-not, restrict). Both sit in the same sentence quoting the conduct standard, so they are one unit. The page reports a rule that binds students and states approval is required, so the final code is student, must-not, restrict (banned unless the instructor approves), P36.

units.why: The Writing Program is quoted: "Communicate clear guidelines and expectations regarding the use of AI writing technology". An instructor should state expectations, P09.
units.anchor: Communicate clear guidelines and expectations regarding the use of AI writing technology

units.why: The same quote calls for "proper, clear, and continual attribution of any use of AI writing tools". That is a disclosure requirement, P24, framed as a suggestion.
units.anchor: proper, clear, and continual attribution of any use of AI writing tools

units.why: "it is very important that you talk about your Gen AI policies in class and with your teaching assistants" asks instructors to explain policies; P66.
units.anchor: it is very important that you talk about your Gen AI policies in class

units.why: Instructors should "consider making some common ground rules with students about what is and isn't acceptable", i.e. setting expectations with students: P67.
units.anchor: making some common ground rules with students about what is and isn’t acceptable

units.why: The same sentence mentions "how students should disclose their use of AI to study", asking instructors to settle a disclosure rule with students. P24.
units.anchor: how students should disclose their use of AI to study
units.fit_note: Stated as a topic for instructors to agree with students, not a fixed requirement.
units.resolution_why: Only coder A coded this. It is the same sentence as the 'common ground rules' unit but names a separate matter, 'how students should disclose their use of AI', so it is a distinct disclosure rule. Kept as P24 should. The page frames it as something for instructors to agree with students, so it stays an instructor-addressed recommendation (see fit_note).

units.why: "Do you have any stipulations about the TA using AI for tasks related to their role as TA?" asks instructors to set limits on TA AI use, P59.
units.anchor: stipulations about the TA using AI for tasks related to their role as TA
units.fit_note: Posed as a question for instructors to settle with TAs.

units.why: The page says "There are many ethical ways that you can use AI to improve your own efficiency" for course preparation and lists prompts (rubric, study guide). Instructor AI use for teaching work, P59, modality may.
units.anchor: many ethical ways that you can use AI to improve your own efficiency
units.resolution_why: Same sentence ('many ethical ways that you can use AI to improve your own efficiency'). Modality may and P59 agreed. Unit stance differed: A permit, B encourage. The page recommends course preparation as 'one that many people find most useful' and offers prompts, which goes beyond bare permission, so encourage.

units.why: Rubric Generator prompt: 'give the AI your assignment instructions, and let it create a rubric'. Instructor use of AI to draft a rubric: P59.
units.anchor: give the AI your assignment instructions, and let it create a rubric for you.
units.resolution_why: Only coder B coded the Rubric Generator prompt ('give the AI your assignment instructions, and let it create a rubric for you'). It is one of the page's suggested AI uses for instructors preparing a course, so it is a real recommendation and is kept as P59, may, encourage.

units.why: Students "should talk to the instructor or TA about which of these ideas may help you" if the instructor has not addressed AI. That is ask-first, P10.
units.anchor: you should talk to the instructor or TA about which of these ideas
units.frag_end: critical thinking you should be practicing
units.resolution_why: Same sentence ('you should talk to the instructor or TA about which of these ideas'). Phase differed: A during-work, B course-start. The student acts when the instructor has not addressed AI in assignments and the student is deciding how to use AI on their work, so during-work. Actor student and P10 agreed.

units.why: The "Socratic Tutor" prompt, "let the AI tutor you with a series of questions", offers AI as a tutor for studying. P12.
units.anchor: let the AI tutor you with a series of questions that adapt to your understanding.

units.why: The "Copy Editor" prompt "doesn't write from scratch for you, but it will give you feedback on things like style, clarity and flow". That allows AI editing support, P91.
units.anchor: doesn’t write from scratch for you, but it will give you feedback

units.why: Innovation Incubator 'helps you bring your creative ideas to life as it guides you in creating a plan for your projects'. Brainstorming support: P15.
units.anchor: helps you bring your creative ideas to life
units.resolution_why: Only coder B coded the Innovation Incubator prompt ('helps you bring your creative ideas to life'). It is on the same list of study prompts offered to students as the Socratic Tutor and Copy Editor that both coders coded, so it is kept as P15, may, encourage.

units.why: The page says Gen AI platforms "use the content that we put into them to train the models". This warns about data use, P50.
units.anchor: they also use the content that we put into them to train the models
units.resolution_why: Same sentence ('they also use the content that we put into them to train the models'). Phase differed: A general, B during-work. The sentence states a fact about how AI platforms work and is not tied to a stage of the work, so general. Actor all, informs and P50 agreed.

units.why: "If you do not wish for your content to be included in the training data, here are ways you can change this setting" points users to privacy settings, P50.
units.anchor: If you do not wish for your content to be included in the training data
units.resolution_why: Only coder A coded this. 'If you do not wish for your content to be included in the training data, here are ways you can change this setting' tells users they may opt out of training use. It is a real privacy provision and is kept as P50, may.

documents.title: Academic Integrity (Student Conduct)
documents.stance_why: The page lists "utilizing artificial intelligence programs without prior approval from instructor" and "Unauthorized use of artificial intelligence programs" as plagiarism, so AI is banned unless the instructor approves.
documents.summary: Student Conduct academic-integrity page. It lists academic dishonesty categories and puts unapproved AI use under plagiarism.

units.why: The page states a general integrity standard: "must represent a student's original work". It binds students and sets a principle, so P29 (own what you submit), modality must, phase general.
units.anchor: Any submission that fulfills an academic requirement must represent a student’s original work.
units.resolution_why: Same sentence ('Any submission that fulfills an academic requirement must represent a student's original work'). Phase differed: A general, B during-work. It is a standard of the Student Conduct Code stated for all submissions, not tied to a stage of the work, so general. Student, must and P29 agreed.

units.why: The plagiarism list includes "utilizing artificial intelligence programs without prior approval from instructor", so AI is off unless the instructor approves. That is a fallback rule (P06) rather than a tier or a misconduct classification; the misconduct label is coded in the next unit.
units.anchor: utilizing artificial intelligence programs without prior approval from instructor
units.resolution_why: Same passage (plagiarism list: 'utilizing artificial intelligence programs without prior approval from instructor'). A: P06, phase general. B: P36, phase when-misuse. The next bullet ('Unauthorized use of artificial intelligence programs') is the unit that labels the offense, so this one is coded for the rule it adds: AI is not allowed without the instructor's prior approval, which is a default (P06) rather than a classification. Phase general because it states the standing rule. Student, must-not and restrict agreed. P36 would also be defensible because the passage sits in a plagiarism list (see fit_note).

units.why: The category "Unauthorized use of artificial intelligence programs to complete course work" is listed under Plagiarism, so it classifies unauthorized AI use as academic dishonesty. P36 fits; P06 does not because this unit labels the offense rather than stating the default.
units.anchor: Unauthorized use of artificial intelligence programs to complete course work
units.resolution_why: Same bullet ('Unauthorized use of artificial intelligence programs to complete course work'). Phase differed: A when-misuse, B during-work. It is a listed category of academic dishonesty, so it classifies misconduct: when-misuse. Both coders gave unit stance prohibit; 'unauthorized' means AI is allowed when authorized, so the final unit stance is restrict. Student, must-not and P36 agreed.

documents.unit: Executive Vice Chancellor and Provost / OTL
documents.title: Guidance Regarding AI-Writing Assistance Technologies
documents.stance_why: The memo says "student use of AI-assistive technology for writing is not allowed ... unless specifically allowed by the instructor or supervisor", a default ban with instructor permission, while telling instructors to choose their own policy.
documents.summary: A 2023 provost-office memo from OTL. It sets writing AI as not allowed unless the instructor permits, advises against detectors, restricts AI grading to UCSB-supported tools, and suggests assignment redesign and classroom uses.

units.why: The memo opens by naming "opportunities and challenges" of AI-assistive technologies for "writing, coding, drawing, and completing equations", which defines what the guidance covers. P61 (define scope) fits; it is not a rule.
units.anchor: including those that assist with forms of composing like writing, coding, drawing, and completing equations
units.frag_start: UCSB’s Office of Teaching and Learning recognizes

units.why: The memo says it gives "guidance about the ethical use of these technologies by both instructors and students", which states purpose and audience. P56 (institution-level framework/preamble) is the closest type.
units.anchor: guidance about the ethical use of these technologies by both instructors and students
units.resolution_why: Only coder A coded this. 'guidance about the ethical use of these technologies by both instructors and students' states the memo's scope and whom it addresses, which is a real scope statement (P56).

units.why: Item 1 is headed "Communicate expectations for student use of AI-writing assistive technologies", telling instructors to state expectations. That is P09 (state AI expectations), modality should since the memo calls it guidance.
units.anchor: Communicate expectations for student use of AI-writing assistive technologies in courses

units.why: The memo places AI writing technologies "within the purview of the Student Conduct Code and the Student Guide to Academic Integrity", so unauthorized use is handled under integrity rules. That is P36.
units.anchor: falls within the purview of the Student Conduct Code
units.resolution_why: Same sentence ('falls within the purview of the Student Conduct Code'). Phase differed: A when-misuse, B general. The sentence places AI-writing use under the conduct code, which is the basis for treating unauthorized use as misconduct (P36), so when-misuse. Actor all, informs and P36 agreed.

units.why: 'student use of AI-assistive technology for writing is not allowed ... unless specifically allowed by the instructor' sets a default ban with instructor permission as the exception. P06 (fallback rule) chosen over P01 because the emphasis is what applies absent instructor permission.
units.anchor: student use of AI-assistive technology for writing is not allowed in courses
units.policy: Student use of AI-assistive technology for writing is not allowed in courses unless specifically allowed by the instructor or supervisor.
units.fit_note: Rule names writing only, although the memo scope includes coding. / Default ban stated for writing in courses; not tied to a silent syllabus explicitly.
units.resolution_why: Same sentence ('student use of AI-assistive technology for writing is not allowed in courses ... unless specifically allowed by the instructor or supervisor'). Actor, phase, modality, unit stance and P06 agreed. The normalized policy follows B's wording because the anchor stops before 'unless'. The coding of theses and research articles is a separate unit.

units.why: The same sentence extends the ban to 'theses, dissertations, research articles' unless the supervisor allows. This is a research-scholarship rule, so P62; the course default is coded separately.
units.anchor: on theses, dissertations, research articles, etc. unless specifically allowed by the instructor or supervisor
units.policy: Student use of AI-assistive technology for writing is not allowed on theses, dissertations, research articles, etc. unless specifically allowed by the supervisor.
units.resolution_why: Only coder B coded the second scope of the default ban: not allowed 'on theses, dissertations, research articles, etc. unless specifically allowed by the instructor or supervisor'. It extends the default rule to research and scholarship (P62), a different setting from courses, so it is a distinct unit and kept.

units.why: "Explain 'why.'" tells instructors to give students reasons for whatever AI rule they set, because AI is "increasingly" integrated into common programs. P66 (explain and discuss rules) fits; modality should as guidance.
units.anchor: important for instructors to explain why and how AI tools should/should not be used

units.why: Lists considerations to explain: 'developing students' critical thoughts/voice/skills'. It gives the learning rationale for limiting AI, so P41.
units.anchor: developing students' critical thoughts/voice/skills
units.policy: Considerations in explaining AI rules include developing students' critical thoughts/voice/skills.
units.resolution_why: Same passage ('developing students' critical thoughts/voice/skills'). Phase differed: A general, B course-start. It names one of the considerations for the 'explain why' step in the course-start communication guidance, so course-start. Instructor, informs and P41 agreed, but the memo only lists skill development as a consideration for explaining rules; it does not say AI shortcuts practice (see fit_note).

units.why: "Consider including a policy statement specifically about the use of AI tools" asks instructors to put an AI statement in the syllabus, and points to sample language. P09 fits; modality should.
units.anchor: Consider including a policy statement specifically about the use of AI tools

units.why: "UCSB does not support the use of plagiarism detection software (e.g. Turnitin, ChatGPT Zero)" is an institutional position against detectors, which is P39. Modality should-not because it is guidance that instructors should not rely on them.
units.anchor: UCSB does not support the use of plagiarism detection software
units.resolution_why: Same sentence ('UCSB does not support the use of plagiarism detection software'). A: instructor, should-not. B: all, must-not. 'Does not support' states an institutional position rather than a prohibition and the guidance is addressed to instructors, so instructor and should-not. Phase when-misuse and P39 agreed.

units.why: Gives the reason that 'Anti-plagiarism software is highly fallible' and detection is 'always one step behind'. Reliability reasons for not using detectors: P39.
units.anchor: Anti-plagiarism software is highly fallible.
units.resolution_why: Same passage (detection software is unreliable). A anchored 'detection software always one step behind what LLMs can produce' and coded P82, phase general; B anchored 'Anti-plagiarism software is highly fallible.' and coded P39, phase when-misuse. The statement's point is that detectors cannot be relied on, which is exactly P39; P82 (AI use cannot be prevented or verified) fits the arms-race clause less well. Phase when-misuse because detectors are used when misuse is suspected.

units.why: The memo warns that uploading student work to a detector "may violate students' intellectual property rights" and the student "may lose ownership". This is about ownership of inputs, so P52 is nearest although it concerns student work rather than AI output.
units.anchor: Submitting student work to anti-plagiarism software may violate students’ intellectual property rights.
units.fit_note: P52 covers ownership of AI inputs and outputs; this says student work uploaded to a detector may lose its student ownership.

units.why: Says detector use 'can undermine the fundamental relationship of trust' between learners and teachers. A further reason against detectors: P39.
units.anchor: Use of anti-plagiarism software can undermine the fundamental relationship of trust
units.fit_note: Detection software is said to damage the trust relationship between learners and teachers, which the type does not capture. (Coder A used UNCOVERED for this: 'Detection software is said to damage the trust relationship between students and instructors.')
units.resolution_why: Same sentence ('Use of anti-plagiarism software can undermine the fundamental relationship of trust'). A: UNCOVERED, actor all, phase general. B: P39, instructor, when-misuse. It is a stated reason for not using detectors, so it fits P39 (do not rely on detectors) partly; the trust rationale is kept in fit_note. Actor instructor and phase when-misuse follow the section the sentence belongs to (instructor use of detection).

units.why: The memo urges moving "from detection of LLM use to prevention" by letting students use LLMs as a tool or crafting assignments "that cannot be produced by LLMs". That is redesigning assignments around AI, P35, modality should (it says instructors "can consider").
units.anchor: craft assignments and activities that cannot be produced by LLMs

units.why: "Office of Teaching and Learning instructional consultants offer extensive support" for instructors changing assignments. That is support for faculty, P63.
units.anchor: instructional consultants offer extensive support for instructors who would like to pursue this approach
units.resolution_why: Same sentence ('instructional consultants offer extensive support for instructors'). A: instructor, B: admin. The sentence says what OTL offers rather than telling instructors to do something, so admin. Phase before-course, informs and P63 agreed.

units.why: 'Instructors and TAs should not use AI-assistive technology for grading and feedback unless the technology is supported by UCSB' allows it only for vetted, contracted tools (Gradescope). Conditions on AI grading: P101 rather than P46 since it does not say only humans grade.
units.anchor: Instructors and TAs should not use AI-assistive technology for grading and feedback unless
units.policy: Instructors and TAs should not use AI-assistive technology for grading and feedback unless the technology is supported by UCSB.
units.fit_note: Allows grading AI only if UCSB-supported; names Gradescope as the example.
units.resolution_why: Same sentence ('Instructors and TAs should not use AI-assistive technology for grading and feedback unless ...'). Actor differed: A ta-staff, B instructor. It binds both; instructor is the first-named and the audience of the memo. Phase during-work, should-not, restrict and P101 agreed. A's fit note (grading AI is allowed only if UCSB-supported, e.g. GradeScope) is kept.

units.why: The same sentence lets staff use UCSB-supported tools such as GradeScope "vetted for FERPA compliance". This stands for the use-approved-tools rule, P92, with a privacy reason.
units.anchor: use of GradeScope is permitted, as UCSB has a contract for its use
units.resolution_why: Only coder A coded this. 'use of GradeScope is permitted, as UCSB has a contract for its use' is a separate permission (an approved tool for grading) in the same sentence as the grading restriction, so it is kept as P92. Actor set to instructor to match the grading restriction it qualifies (A had ta-staff).

units.why: "If you suspect unauthorized use of AI technologies, submit an incident report" gives the formal route to the Office of Student Conduct. P81 (follow the reporting procedure), modality should.
units.anchor: If you suspect unauthorized use of AI technologies, submit an

units.why: The memo tells instructors to 'include any samples of earlier/baseline student writing to which the writing in question can be compared' when reporting suspected misuse. That says what evidence supports an AI-misuse report, so P69 (evidence for misuse findings) fits; P40 (tools and logs used to identify misuse) fits less well because no tool or log is named. Instructor, when-misuse, should.
units.anchor: include any samples of earlier/baseline student writing
units.fit_note: Names earlier/baseline student writing as the comparison evidence to attach to an incident report; the type is about evidence standards for finding misuse. (Coder A used P40, noting it names baseline writing samples attached to an incident report rather than similarity checks and logs.)
units.resolution_why: Same sentence ('include any samples of earlier/baseline student writing'). A: P40. B: P69. The unit says what evidence to submit with an incident report, which is an evidence standard (P69), not a detection method (P40). Actor, phase and modality agreed.

units.why: "Scaffold writing assignments" in smaller pieces with feedback is a design change to avoid AI problems, P35.
units.anchor: Scaffold writing assignments, so that students are writing smaller pieces

units.why: "Add brief reflective writing to assignments that ask students to analyze the choices that they made" is an assignment redesign (P35); it is not a requirement to submit AI logs (P26).
units.anchor: Add brief reflective writing to assignments that ask students to analyze the choices

units.why: "Talk with students about the purpose of writing in the course and work with students to use LLMs in productive ways" is about explaining and discussing, P66.
units.anchor: Talk with students about the purpose of writing in the course

units.why: "Assign topics that require personal reflection or creative thinking" is an assignment redesign to avoid AI problems, P35.
units.anchor: Assign topics that require personal reflection or creative thinking.

units.why: Item 5 invites instructors to "Create assignments where students use LLMs as part of the writing/thinking activities". That builds AI into coursework, P79; modality should since it says "Consider".
units.anchor: Create assignments where students use LLMs as part of the writing/thinking activities.
units.fit_note: Instructors are invited, not required, to build AI use into assignments.
units.resolution_why: Same sentence ('Create assignments where students use LLMs as part of the writing/thinking activities'). Modality differed: A should, B may. It sits under 'Consider incorporating AI Writing Assistance technologies into your course' and is phrased as an imperative suggestion, so should. P79 and encourage agreed.

units.why: "Stimulate discussions about writing processes, strategies, and ethics through discussions of AI writing technology" asks instructors to discuss AI with students (P66).
units.anchor: Stimulate discussions about writing processes, strategies, and ethics

units.why: The memo suggests using AI writing technology "to create prompts, topics, or questions for exploration", which is brainstorming and exploring, P15.
units.anchor: leveraging AI writing technology to create prompts, topics, or questions for exploration

units.why: 'Invite students to utilize AI to generate text in specific genres' to study genre conventions: AI built into coursework, P79.
units.anchor: Invite students to utilize AI to generate text in specific genres
units.resolution_why: Only coder B coded 'Invite students to utilize AI to generate text in specific genres'. It is a separate recommendation in the same list of ways to build AI into the course, so kept as P79, should, encourage.

units.why: 'compare AI-generated text with human-generated text' as a classroom activity: P79 (AI-use built into an activity).
units.anchor: Encourage students to compare AI-generated text with human-generated text
units.resolution_why: Only coder B coded 'Encourage students to compare AI-generated text with human-generated text'. It is a separate recommendation in the same list, so kept as P79, should, encourage.

units.why: The memo says LLMs "can hallucinate" and "Urge students to cross-check AI-generated information". That is verify-the-output, P31.
units.anchor: Urge students to cross-check AI-generated information and develop critical appraisal skills

units.why: The memo asks instructors to "Examine and address potential biases and fairness concerns" including "perpetuation of stereotypes". That names bias as a harm, P53.
units.anchor: Examine and address potential biases and fairness concerns that may arise from AI writing technology

units.why: "Think about your course objectives. What are the cognitive tasks students need to perform without AI assistance?" ties AI decisions to learning objectives, P83.
units.anchor: What are the cognitive tasks students need to perform without AI assistance?
units.policy: Instructors think about their course objectives, including what cognitive tasks students need to perform without AI assistance.
units.resolution_why: Same passage (course objectives and cognitive tasks without AI assistance). A anchored the question 'What are the cognitive tasks students need to perform without AI assistance?'; B anchored 'Think about your course objectives.' Actor instructor, phase before-course, should and P83 agreed. A normalized policy was written so the instruction and the question are both stated.

notes: No school or computing-unit policy found; course layer deferred. The OTL page names no computing-specific rule. Memo is from 2023 and may be partly superseded; the page says UCSB has no formal AI policy as of Summer 2025. Topic codes are free-form descriptive tags (no list file found). | Coder B: Scenario questions in the OTL page and external resource lists were not coded as policies. The EVC memo (2023) may be partly superseded by the OTL AI 101 page (2025). Several OTL units use P63/P66/P04 with fit notes. | Reconciler: california-santa-barbara-otl-ai101: dropped only-A unit (A0): scope statement of the AI 101 series ('navigate how to use, or not use, AI'). california-santa-barbara-otl-ai101: dropped only-A unit (A4): 'Join the AI Community of Practice' is a navigation link. california-santa-barbara-otl-ai101: dropped only-A unit (A9): equity scenario about a paid subscription is a scenario prompt, not a statement of policy (A note: presented as a scenario to think through, not as a requirement to provide access). california-santa-barbara-otl-ai101: dropped only-A unit (A18): 'How will you be communicating this policy to students?' is a discussion question (A note: phrased as discussion questions for instructor and TA, not a mandate). california-santa-barbara-otl-ai101: dropped only-A unit (A20): 'If a TA should encounter work with blatant cheating or plagiarism, what should they do?' is a discussion question (A note: a question to plan for, not a stated procedure). california-santa-barbara-otl-ai101: dropped only-B unit (B1): 'AI 102 covers the Fundamentals of AI Literacy' is series navigation (B note: describes a series of OTL pages rather than a mandated training). california-santa-barbara-otl-ai101: dropped only-B unit (B13): 'What is AI good for in this class?' is a conversation-starter question, not a statement; the surrounding sentence about talking with students is coded. california-santa-barbara-otl-ai101: dropped only-B unit (B17): 'prompt engineering basics for teachers' is a resource link. california-santa-barbara-conduct: dropped only-B unit (B3): 'Using any unauthorized material such as notes, cheat sheets, or electronic devices during an exam' does not mention AI (B note: does not mention AI; covers unauthorized electronic devices on exams generally). california-santa-barbara-evc-memo: dropped only-A unit (A28): 'Learn Prompting' is a resource link. Scenario prompts and discussion questions on the OTL page were not coded as policies unless they stated a rule. Topic codes are descriptive tags merged from both coders.
